card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two-mana rock that always makes a usable color. Unglamorous, reliable.
card_roles.Ashnod's Altar: A free outlet that turns bodies into {C}{C}, which is real acceleration in a deck making free tokens. Its famous Mikaeus pairing is refuted; its Skullclamp pairing is a combo-graph entry and does what it says.
card_roles.Bastion of Remembrance: Table-wide drain in enchantment form, so a wrath cannot touch it, and it brings its own body. One of three cards the build plan classifies as a dedicated wincon.
card_roles.Birds of Paradise: A one-drop that fixes both colors and, being a creature, is also fodder, a blocker and a Skullclamp target.
card_roles.Bitterblossom: A free body every upkeep for 1 life. Faerie Rogues are Skullclamp fodder, sacrifice fodder and chump blockers, and it rebuilds through wraths on its own.
card_roles.Black Sun's Zenith: Not a reset button but a rebuild: X counters on *each* creature triggers Hapatra once per creature, feeds Nest of Scarabs, and hands Necroskitter every opposing creature that dies with a counter on it.
card_roles.Blasting Station: An outlet that is also a converter — it untaps whenever a creature enters, so a token stream turns it into repeatable damage with no drain payoff needed. Refuted as a Mikaeus two-card infinite.
card_roles.Blood Artist: Drains one *target player* per death, not each opponent, so treat it as a value card and a wrath-tax rather than a table clock. Verified in stack 001 as converting the Druid loop at one life per cycle.
card_roles.Blowfly Infestation: The headline two-card kill on paper — 16.3% assembled per goldfish — and unverified. Even setting the loop aside, it is a mandatory counter placement every time any creature dies with a counter on it, which is a genuine repeating source for Hapatra in ordinary games.
card_roles.Carrion Feeder: A free outlet, and actively anti-synergistic with Mikaeus: it puts +1/+1 counters on itself, which is precisely what undying will not tolerate. Refuted as a Mikaeus infinite.
card_roles.Chrome Mox: Free acceleration that eats a colored card from your hand. A Game Changer, and the card you exile is a real cost in a deck this dense with singleton answers.
card_roles.Contagion Clasp: A counter on entry and a repeatable proliferate. Slow, but it is a permanent source in a deck that is short on repeatable sources.
card_roles.Crumbling Ashes: Upkeep-triggered destruction of any creature with a -1/-1 counter on it. In a deck that sprays counters, this is repeating unconditional removal.
card_roles.Dark Ritual: Three black off one, and the classic way to land Hapatra on turn 1 or Yawgmoth ahead of curve.
card_roles.Deadly Dispute: Instant-speed two cards plus a Treasure for a body you were going to lose anyway. Classified as draw, not ramp — the Treasure is a rider.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: The cleanest tutor in the format and a Game Changer. Fetch a repeatable counter source first, a table-wide converter second.
card_roles.Devoted Druid: Half of the deck's one verified two-card infinite. Its untap ability pays a -1/-1 counter as a cost, which is a free repeatable counter source in disguise, and under Mikaeus it resets itself forever — for deaths and Snakes, not mana.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: Any card to hand, with a body as the additional cost — which is nearly free here, because the body was fodder and its death is a trigger.
card_roles.Elvish Mystic: The fourth copy of the same effect. In a deck where the commander costs two and lands on turn 2 in 99.9% of runs, this is what makes turn 1 possible.
card_roles.Eternal Witness: Rebuys the tutor, the sweeper or the combo piece that got answered, on a body that is itself sacrifice fodder.
card_roles.Fixing lands: Bayou, Command Tower, City of Brass, Mana Confluence, Exotic Orchard, Spire of Industry, Conduit Pylons, Gond Gate, Hidden Grotto, Darkbore Pathway, Wastewood Verge, The Grey Havens, Tarnished Citadel, Forbidden Orchard and Gemstone Caverns fill out a 36-land base with zero lands entering tapped, 29 sources of each color against a target of 22, and 96.2% on-curve for both pips. Forbidden Orchard gives an opponent a Spirit each time you tap it — that Spirit is also a legal target for your own -1/-1 counters.
card_roles.Flourishing Defenses: A third mint on the same trigger, making an Elf Warrior on every -1/-1 placement. The deck's only five-drop, and a combo-graph Blowfly partner whose loop is unresolved.
card_roles.Fume Spitter: A one-mana, free, instant-speed -1/-1 source — a Snake, a dead X/1, and a body for a sacrifice cost, all for one card.
card_roles.Green Sun's Zenith: Fetches a green creature straight onto the battlefield — Devoted Druid or Ivy Lane Denizen with the tempo attached rather than a card in hand.
card_roles.Grim Affliction: Instant-speed counter placement plus proliferate, so it can be a Snake at flash speed or a second counter on something already shrinking.
card_roles.Grim Haruspex: Draws on every nontoken creature you control dying, which is what makes the sacrifice half of the deck free rather than costly. Morph gives it a floor when you need a body more than a trigger.
card_roles.Grim Monolith: Three colorless with a {4} untap. A Game Changer; note that neither Vault nor Monolith makes colored mana, and this deck's costs are pip-heavy.
card_roles.Grim Tutor: Any card to hand for three mana and 3 life. Not a Game Changer, and the price is real in a deck that pays life everywhere else.
card_roles.Hapatra, Vizier of Poisons: The mint. Her second ability converts any -1/-1 counter placement into a 1/1 deathtouch Snake, once per event rather than per counter; her combat trigger is a bonus on an unevasive 2/2 and never a plan (verified stack 001, step 11).
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Hexproof and indestructible for your whole board at instant speed. The one card that beats a targeted answer to your combo piece and a wrath at the same time.
card_roles.Host of the Hereafter: Moves counters from a dying creature onto another creature you control. Its only combo-graph partner in the entire graph is Hapatra, and whether moving counters counts as *putting* them is exactly the unresolved question.
card_roles.Imperial Seal: Sorcery-speed Vampiric Tutor. A Game Changer, and slow enough that you want it early rather than at the pivot.
card_roles.Ivy Lane Denizen: Puts a +1/+1 counter on target creature whenever another green creature you control enters. Six of the listed infinites pair it with sacrifice outlets that make nothing enter, which is why those six read as projection artifacts. Unverified either way.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Protection and haste for {0} equip — and the specific card that restores mana to the Devoted Druid loop, netting four green per cycle as a main-phase-only three-card line. Its shroud shuts Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting the equipped creature.
card_roles.Llanowar Elves: Turn-1 acceleration to a turn-2 Hapatra, and a body the deck can eat later.
card_roles.Lotus Petal: One free mana of any color, once. The card that makes an explosive keep functional rather than aspirational.
card_roles.Mana Vault: Three mana off a one-drop with an untap tax and upkeep damage. A Game Changer, and pure speed — spend it on a turn that matters.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: The combo hinge and a trap in one card. Undying on every other non-Human creature enables the two verified lines, while the same +1/+1 anthem keeps a counterless Walking Ballista alive at 1/1 and may switch off your own token loops — an open question flagged above.
card_roles.Morbid Opportunist: Once-per-turn card advantage off any creatures dying, including your opponents'. Cheap insurance that a sweeper turns into a card.
card_roles.Mox Diamond: Free acceleration that eats a land. A Game Changer, and it makes any color, which is what separates it from the colorless rocks.
card_roles.Necroskitter: Turns a shrunken opposing board into your board — any creature an opponent controls that dies with a -1/-1 counter on it comes back under your control. It is verified *absent* from the combo graph, so treat the Black Sun's Zenith pairing as strong oracle reasoning rather than a confirmed line.
card_roles.Nest of Scarabs: A parallel mint: it reads *that many* Insects, so it scales with counter volume in a way Hapatra does not. Listed as an in-deck Blowfly partner in the combo graph; that pairing is unverified.
card_roles.Night's Whisper: Unconditional two-for-one at two mana. Life is a resource this deck spends freely.
card_roles.Obelisk Spider: The best converter in the deck and the correct tutor target when you already have a source. It drains each opponent on counter *placement* rather than on death, so it converts a counter loop several times faster than any death-trigger drain.
card_roles.Orcish Bowmasters: A flash body that pings on entry and again on every extra opponent draw, and amasses Orcs. A Game Changer, and a rare piece of instant-speed interaction in a list that has very little.
card_roles.Phyrexian Altar: A free outlet producing colored mana, which matters more than Ashnod's colorless in a BG deck with double-pip costs. Refuted as a Mikaeus infinite.
card_roles.Phyrexian Reclamation: Repeatable creature recursion for {1}{B} and 2 life — the answer to targeted removal on Yawgmoth or Mikaeus, and unkillable by creature removal.
card_roles.Pitiless Plunderer: Turns every other creature you control dying into a Treasure, which is how the sacrifice half of the deck pays for itself. A combo-graph in-deck Skullclamp partner.
card_roles.Scurry Oak: Makes a Squirrel whenever one or more +1/+1 counters are put on it. Its pairing with Ivy Lane Denizen is what the bracket engine called the deck's highest-bracket line — and stack 001 deliberately declined to rest the bracket floor on it. Unverified.
card_roles.Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER // Sephiroth,: Sacrifice-for-a-card on entry and on attack, plus a drain on every other creature dying that transforms on the fourth resolution. The synergy graph lists it as an in-deck Hapatra partner at score 4 (Tokens + Sacrifice, -1/-1 + Death Trigger, Flying + Damage Trigger, Attack Trigger + Tokens).
card_roles.Serrated Arrows: Three counters across three turns from a colorless permanent — three Snakes and three shrinks, no colored pips required.
card_roles.Skullclamp: The bodies-to-cards engine. Every Snake, Insect, Faerie and Elf Warrior is a 1/1, so this is 'pay {1}, draw two' on repeat. Combo-graph in-deck partners include Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Mikaeus and Pitiless Plunderer.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colorless on turn one, which is what turns a turn-2 Hapatra into a turn-2 Hapatra plus a play.
card_roles.Survival of the Fittest: Repeatable creature filtering for {G} and a discard, which in a deck with Phyrexian Reclamation and Eternal Witness is barely a cost. A Game Changer and the most powerful tutor in the list.
card_roles.Swiftfoot Boots: Hexproof and haste that still allows your own targeting. On the Druid loop it nets only three green per cycle, because the {1} equip must be paid again every cycle after the Equipment falls off.
card_roles.The One Ring: Protection from everything for a turn when cast, then an escalating draw engine. A Game Changer, and the burden counters are a real cost in a deck already paying life to Yawgmoth, Bitterblossom and three painlands.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: The pure reset, and the sharp caveat. It gives -X/-X until end of turn and places no counters at all, so it triggers neither Hapatra nor Nest of Scarabs nor Necroskitter. Sequence it as the emergency button it is.
card_roles.Utility lands: Grim Backwoods, Lazotep Quarry and Grim Backwoods' fellow travellers give you sacrifice outlets and card draw off lands; Svogthos, the Restless Tomb is a late-game creature-land off a full graveyard; Opal Palace grows Hapatra past commander tax; Talon Gates of Madara phases out a creature on entry; The Mycosynth Gardens copies an artifact; Abstergo Entertainment is the deck's only graveyard-touching effect. Note Lazotep Quarry is the eighth mana-free outlet in the verified census — {T} with no untapper, so once per turn and unable to loop.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Instant-speed any card to the top for 2 life. A Game Changer; costs you a draw step, so use it on the turn the answer matters.
card_roles.Village Rites: One mana, sacrifice a creature, draw two at instant speed. The cheapest way to turn a Snake into cards in response to removal.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: A free outlet with library smoothing attached. Refuted as a Mikaeus infinite — one return, then the +1/+1 counter shuts it down.
card_roles.Walking Ballista: Removal that scales and a verified kill piece with Mikaeus plus any free outlet. Note that Mikaeus's anthem stops it from killing itself, so it needs the third card; without Mikaeus it is your best answer to a single problem creature.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: Instant-speed creature to the top — Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, Necroskitter or a converter. A Game Changer.
card_roles.Yahenni, Undying Partisan: A free sacrifice outlet on a hasty body that can protect itself with indestructible. One of the six Mikaeus pairings stack 001 refuted — it gives one undying return, not a loop.
card_roles.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: The deck's only free repeatable -1/-1 source and therefore the tutor target that matters. Pay 1 life, sac another creature, place a counter, draw — but the single 'target' means an illegal target fizzles the whole ability, so a second body is mandatory. Library-bounded by its own mandatory draw.
card_roles.Zulaport Cutthroat: A table-wide converter — each opponent loses 1 life per creature you control dying. This is the class that closes games; Blood Artist is not a substitute for it.

combo_lines.001:
This is the scenario that rewrote the deck. Nineteen two-card infinites were counted; eight of them routed through Mikaeus, the Unhallowed plus a free sacrifice outlet, and the claim under test was that Hapatra supplies the missing reset — that her -1/-1 counter annihilates the +1/+1 counter undying returns a creature with, making it a legal undying target forever. Four resolver passes and four adversarial checks later (checker verdict: pass), the claim is FALSE as written, and the wreckage is more useful than the claim would have been.

What survives, verified. **Mikaeus + Devoted Druid is a true two-card infinite** — of deaths, -1/-1 placements, Snakes and drain, and explicitly **not of mana**. The Druid's untap ability pays a -1/-1 counter as a cost, so it kills itself into a counterless graveyard and undying returns it cleanly. Read the mana line carefully, because everyone gets it wrong: the returned Druid is a *new object* that has not been under your control since your turn began, so 302.6 forbids its {T} ability. You get three green on the first pass and **zero on every pass after**. The loop still runs forever, because the untap cost carries no tap or untap symbol and sits outside 302.6 entirely. Steady state without haste: four counter placements, one death, zero mana per cycle — which is four Snakes a cycle with Hapatra out, one drain a cycle with Blood Artist, and four drains a cycle with Obelisk Spider. Bolt on Lightning Greaves and the mana comes back as a **three-card, main-phase-only** line netting four green per cycle; Swiftfoot Boots nets only three, because the Equipment falls off the moment the Druid dies and must be re-equipped every single cycle, and equip is sorcery-speed. Greaves also hands the Druid shroud, which locks Hapatra and Yawgmoth out of targeting it — know which you want before you fetch.

**Mikaeus + Walking Ballista is real, and it is a three-card line, not two.** Mikaeus's +1/+1 is a layer-7c modification applied alongside counters, so a Ballista with no counters left is a 1/1 under Mikaeus, not a 0/0. It never dies on its own; the classic self-killing pattern is switched off, and an external free outlet is mandatory. With one, it is genuinely unbounded at 1 damage per iteration plus whatever the outlet yields, and it converts to a win with no drain payoff at all.

What died. **Six of the listed infinites are refuted outright.** Mikaeus paired with Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni or Blasting Station yields exactly *one* undying return, not a loop: the creature comes back with a +1/+1 counter, and when you sacrifice it again the intervening 'if' is false and undying never triggers. Total output, four colorless and two drains in the Altar case. Carrion Feeder is actively anti-synergistic — it *adds* +1/+1 counters. And the flagship misconception is worse still: **feeding Snake tokens to Mikaeus produces zero iterations.** State-based actions are performed first as a single event, and a token in a zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist, so the Snake is gone before its undying trigger is even placed on the stack; the trigger then resolves and does nothing. Undying on a token is a dead grant. Any line that reads 'sacrifice a Snake, get it back' is invalid on its face.

One further finding worth the price of the whole scenario: **Yawgmoth loops for real, and it needs a second body.** His counter annihilates an undying +1/+1, so he does not hit the wall the six refuted outlets hit — but the ability has only one instance of the word 'target', so if the creature you targeted is the creature you sacrificed, the whole ability fails to resolve and you do not even draw. Run it as an A/B loop across two non-Human creatures, or let Hapatra's Snakes fill the second slot. Each activation costs 1 life and the draw is mandatory, so it is library-bounded: a strong engine, not a true infinite.

One trap to carry to the table. Counter annihilation *does* reset undying, but only when the annihilation and the death fall in **different** SBA checks. If the -1/-1 counters annihilate and take toughness to 0 in the same check, last known information is read from before any of those actions — the +1/+1 counter is still visible and undying does not trigger. Strip the counter, let state-based actions run, then kill it separately.

And finally, what this scenario deliberately did **not** settle. Eleven of the nineteen listed lines remain unresolved and none of them may be spoken of as fact at your table or ours. The Blowfly Infestation family — Blowfly with Hapatra, with Nest of Scarabs, with Flourishing Defenses — is the deck's headline two-card kill, the one the goldfish tracks at 16.3% assembled and 12.5% by turn 6, and it has never been verified; a scenario must settle whether the loop is optional enough to avoid a draw, whether it needs a seed counter and a spare token, and what happens when no legal target remains. **Needs a stack scenario.** Sharper still: Mikaeus gives other non-Human creatures +1/+1, and Snakes, Insects and Elf Warriors are all non-Human — if that anthem makes your own token fodder too big to die to your own -1/-1 counters, then the deck's two flagship engines are mutually exclusive on the battlefield. **Needs a stack scenario, and it is the highest-value open question in the list.** The Ivy Lane Denizen family is unresolved on both halves: Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen is the entry the bracket engine called the deck's highest-bracket line, and stack 001 pointedly refused to rest the floor on it; the six outlet-paired Ivy Lane entries look like the same projection artifact that inflated the Mikaeus count, since none of those outlets causes a green creature to *enter*. **Needs a stack scenario.** So does Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter — elegant on oracle text, and turning entirely on whether Host's counter-*moving* counts as *putting* counters for Hapatra's trigger. **Needs a stack scenario.** The bracket floor of 4 holds regardless, on the 11 Game Changers plus the three lines verified here. It simply does not hold on the number nineteen.

cover.identity: You are playing a converter, not a combo pile. Hapatra does not make -1/-1 counters at will — her first ability is a combat-damage trigger on an unevasive 2/2 — she monetises counters that *other* cards place, at a rate of one 1/1 deathtouch Snake per placement event. The 99 around her is built so that every counter becomes a body, every body becomes a card or a drain, and a narrow but genuine combo ceiling sits above a very strong grindy median.

how_it_wins:
Start with the sentence that reorganises the whole list: Hapatra is not an engine, she is a mint. Her second ability — 'Whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, create a 1/1 green Snake creature token with deathtouch' — is the passive half that matters, and it is an exchange rate, not a source. It pays out once per placement *event*, not once per counter, so Black Sun's Zenith for three on one creature mints one Snake, while Black Sun's Zenith for one across six creatures mints six. Her first ability is the weak half and should never be a plan: verified stack 001 (step 11) classifies it as a combat-damage trigger that goes on the stack only when a 2/2 with no evasion connects, worth at most one extra iteration per combat. She is, however, the most reliable card you own — the goldfish casts her on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 runs, mean 2.007, 99.9% by turn 6.

Because she is a mint, the scarce card class is the *counter source*, and this is where the deck's real shape lives. Stack 001's adversarial checker re-derived the full census from every 'sacrific' card in the list: eight sacrifice outlets cost no mana (Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni, Yawgmoth, Blasting Station, and Lazotep Quarry once per turn), and exactly *one* of them also places a -1/-1 counter. That is Yawgmoth, Thran Physician. The only other free repeatable source is Devoted Druid, and only while Mikaeus is on the battlefield to reset it. Two cards. Everything downstream — Snakes, Insects, Elf Warriors, Skullclamp draws, Blood Artist drains, Necroskitter steals — is abundant and redundant. The eight tutors are not luxury; they are what makes a two-deep class playable at all, and the goldfish has one drawn in 78.0% of games, 67.6% by turn 6.

The median game, which is most games, wins by out-carding three opponents and then draining them. Snakes are 1/1, so Skullclamp is a two-card draw for {1} on every single one; Grim Haruspex draws off each nontoken death; Deadly Dispute and Village Rites turn a spare body into two cards at instant speed; Morbid Opportunist collects once a turn no matter whose creatures die. Meanwhile every 1/1 deathtouch body is virtual interaction — it blanks an attacker of any size — so the board that is drawing you cards is also the board that makes attacking you unprofitable. The goldfish target that describes this game is 'commander plus any -1/-1 payoff': 67.2% assembled, mean turn 3.62. That is the deck's actual identity.

The ceiling is real but narrower than the bracket sheet suggests, and you should pilot it that way. The kill is a repeatable counter source feeding a converter that hits every seat — Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance or Obelisk Spider, with Blood Artist one tier down because it drains a single target player per death. Obelisk Spider is the outlier worth tutoring for: it drains on counter *placement* rather than on death, so it converts a counter loop roughly four times faster than a death-trigger drain does. Any drain converter is drawn 51.9% of games, 41.5% by turn 6. Pivot when both halves are live and the table's interaction has been counted and spent — not when the board merely looks impressive. And take the honest read on the bracket: the floor of 4 is safe on the 11 Game Changers alone, but the '19 two-card infinites' figure that supplied a third of its justification is inflated, and the next section is where that bill comes due.
matchups:
Against sweeper control you are structurally well-placed and should still sequence like you are not. Your token half is nearly free to lose: Bitterblossom rebuilds every upkeep for 1 life, Skullclamp turns a 1/1 Snake into two cards for {1} (it gives +1/-1, so the Snake dies on equip), Grim Haruspex draws off every nontoken death, and Blood Artist triggers on ANY creature dying — a table wrath with Blood Artist out is a large drain aimed wherever you like. That resilience was bought at deckbuild time, which is exactly what strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math means by buying resilience instead of restraint. The asymmetry runs the other way on your combo half: Hapatra, Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, Ivy Lane Denizen, Scurry Oak and Necroskitter are all creatures, so a wrath is close to one-sided against the half that wins and cheap against the half that grinds. Deploy in waves, lead with tokens and cheap counter sources, and hold the enabler in hand until the pivot window; assume the wrath, because over a four-player game one is near-certain. Your own sweepers are not interchangeable and this is the single most valuable sequencing fact in the matchup: Black Sun's Zenith puts X -1/-1 counters on each creature, so it triggers Hapatra once per creature, feeds Nest of Scarabs, and hands Necroskitter every opposing creature that dies with a counter on it — it is a rebuild, not a reset. Toxic Deluge gives -X/-X until end of turn and places no counters, so it triggers Hapatra, Nest and Necroskitter zero times; it is a pure panic button with an additional cost of X life, and should be sequenced as one. Heroic Intervention is the card that flips this matchup — hold it for the turn you go, not the turn you feel sad — with one caution worth stating plainly: on oracle text it grants hexproof and indestructible, which does not obviously answer a -X/-X effect that kills by toughness rather than destruction. That reading deserves its own stack scenario before you bet a game on it.

Against stax and tax decks the breadth gap gets its bill, and the honest coaching is that you cannot answer the archetype — you race it or you politick it. There is no artifact removal, no enchantment removal and no counterspell in the list, so a Sphere effect, a Winter Orb, a Blood Moon or a graveyard hoser sits there permanently. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite names stax as "the hardest breadth test" and requires that some answers be castable under the tax; yours are not, because you have none of the right class. Three things genuinely favour you anyway. One, you are fast and cheap: 36 lands with zero entering tapped, 11 ramp slots including three zero-cost rocks, and a commander who lands on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 goldfish runs (mean 2.007), so you are frequently under the lock before the second and third pieces layer — and layering is the whole game here, since strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial notes that one piece is an inconvenience while the compounding second and third are the lock. Two, your engines are mana-free once assembled, which is the exact profile that survives a tax: Yawgmoth's activation costs 1 life and a body and no mana, the Devoted Druid loop's steady state produces four counter placements and one death per cycle at zero mana (verified stack 001 step 14), and Bitterblossom triggers on your upkeep for free. Recount your hand under the tax the way that section says, then notice that the part of your deck that wins is the part the tax does not touch. Three, you can tell the truth: strategy:multiplayer.politics warns that credibility is a multi-game resource, so say out loud that you are the seat with no artifact or enchantment answer, and ask the player holding the Krosan Grip to spend it. Keep the deal small, specific and expiring — one turn of your -1/-1 counters pointed elsewhere for one piece of enchantment removal. And know your tutor default has changed: stack 001's final state names the tutor target that matters as a free repeatable -1/-1 source, not any particular altar. A tutor is drawn in 78.0% of games, 67.6% by turn 6, mean turn 2.695 — under an assembling lock, fetch the source, then the converter, and take Green Sun's Zenith for Devoted Druid straight onto the battlefield when you need the tempo.

Against aggro you are favoured, and mostly for a reason that never shows up in a removal count. A 1/1 deathtouch Snake is virtual interaction: it makes attacking into you a losing exchange regardless of the attacker's size, and a board of them turns an opposing creature deck's best cards into cards it cannot profitably use. That is strategy:card-advantage.virtual exactly — "a card that blanks several opposing cards generates advantage without drawing anything" — and the section's Commander correction is the part that matters at a four-player table: virtual advantage triples, because one effect can blank attack plans from three players at once, the cheapest way to answer roughly 120 life worth of aggression. Against trample the Snake still trades up; you eat the overflow and their creature dies to a token that cost you nothing. Goldfish puts mean bodies at 2.101 by turn 4 and 3.224 by turn 6, and that is a floor rather than a ceiling, because the model simulates resource development rather than full games and counts bodies as creatures cast plus tokens parsed from "create ... token" text. Behind the Snakes, Black Sun's Zenith and Toxic Deluge are catch-up buttons, and Necroskitter converts their aggression into your board — it has wither and returns any creature an opponent controls that dies with a -1/-1 counter on it. The frame's read that Necroskitter alongside Black Sun's Zenith is the deck's single best card against a creature table is oracle reasoning only; Necroskitter is verified absent from the combo graph and the pairing has no stack scenario, so plan for it and do not promise it. The real discipline here is life. This deck spends life constantly — Yawgmoth at 1 per activation, Phyrexian Reclamation at 2 per return, Bitterblossom every upkeep, The One Ring's burden counters, Toxic Deluge's additional cost, and City of Brass, Mana Confluence and Tarnished Citadel in the mana base — so your life total is a shared budget with your engine. Track which single opponent's clock is actually real and defend against that one rather than the table (strategy:multiplayer.pod-management). And do not convert a good matchup into a bad seat by attacking with Hapatra into open blockers for a marginal combat trigger.

Against combo you are thin in both directions and should play it as a race rather than an interaction game. You have no counterspell and no way to touch an artifact or enchantment kill, so the only combo decks you can interact with are creature-based — and there you do have instant-speed answers worth holding: Grim Affliction at instant speed, Fume Spitter's free sacrifice, Walking Ballista's counter-removal ping, Serrated Arrows' tap. The answer-economy rule inverts in this matchup: held answers rot, and strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy says the last profitable moment against combo is now. Rank combo proximity above every board threat and re-rank every turn (strategy:threat-assessment). Be honest about your own speed while you do it. 'Any drain converter' is drawn 51.9% of games, 41.5% by turn 6, mean turn 3.339; the Blowfly assembly is 16.3% overall, 12.5% by turn 6, mean turn 4.102 — and that line is unverified, one of eleven unresolved entries. Do not plan to out-speed a dedicated combo deck on raw assembly. Plan instead to be the deck the table's interaction is not pointed at: deploy Snakes that read as defensive, take your window while three players watch each other (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection), and remember the tell — the moment a Mox, a Demonic Tutor or The One Ring hits the table, the cover the Snakes bought you is gone.

Against creature midrange you are in the seat the deck was actually built for, and you out-grind them on two axes simultaneously: their removal is bad against tokens, and their attacks are bad into deathtouch. Hold single-target removal until a threat is pointed at you rather than spending it on sight — strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry is exact about why, since every one-for-one you cast spends a card, costs one opponent a card, and profits two bystanders for free. The card that quietly dominates this matchup is Crumbling Ashes: an enchantment that destroys a creature with a -1/-1 counter on it at the beginning of each of your upkeeps, which with any counter source is a repeatable removal engine sitting in a permanent class most fair creature decks cannot answer either. Seed with Fume Spitter or Grim Affliction, let Ashes do the rest, and note every one of those placements is also a Snake. Meanwhile the bodies-to-cards layer is what wins the long game: Skullclamp, Grim Haruspex, Morbid Opportunist, Deadly Dispute, Village Rites and Sephiroth turn a stream of 1/1s into a stream of cards, and strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock names an engine that scales as a source of inevitability — four-player games trend long, so inevitability compounds and engines are the default winning plan. Then pivot on a counted trigger, not on a pretty board: both halves live means a free repeatable -1/-1 source (Yawgmoth, or Mikaeus with Devoted Druid) plus a converter that hits every seat. Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance and Obelisk Spider each drain every opponent; Blood Artist drains one target player per death, which makes it a value card and a wrath tax rather than a table clock. Obelisk Spider is the one to fetch when the Druid loop is your kill, because it drains on counter placement rather than on death, and stack 001 step 14 puts the no-haste steady state at four placements and one death per cycle — four drains per cycle instead of one.
mulligan:
The keep test is not 'does this hand have a payoff'. It is: **is there a route to a repeatable counter source?** Hapatra mints Snakes from counters other cards place, so a hand full of Nest of Scarabs, Blood Artist and Zulaport Cutthroat with nothing to place a counter is a hand of blanks waiting for a card you have not drawn yet.

The numbers say you can afford to be picky and rarely have to be. The goldfish keeps its first seven 79.9% of the time and averages 0.243 mulligans, casts Hapatra on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 runs (mean 2.007, 99.9% by turn 6), and has a tutor in hand 67.6% of the time by turn 6. So a keep does not need to *contain* the engine — it needs lands, a turn-2 commander, and a card that finds one.

Keep on sight: two to four lands with Hapatra castable on turn 2, plus any of Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, or any of the eight tutors. Keep two-landers with a mana dork or a mox — Birds of Paradise, Llanowar Elves, Elvish Mystic, Sol Ring, Lotus Petal, Dark Ritual — because that hand casts Hapatra on turn 1 or turn 2 with a play attached. Keep hands with Skullclamp and any token maker; Bitterblossom alone is a card every other turn and rebuilds through wraths. Keep Blowfly Infestation as a *counter source*, which is what it reliably is, and not as half of a two-card kill that has never been verified.

Ship these. Hands with five or more lands and no tutor or dork — the curve here has a mean mana value of 2.19 and cannot use the seventh land. Hands whose only action is drain converters (Blood Artist, Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance) with no source and no tutor: those are the blanks the mint metaphor is warning you about. Hands built around Mikaeus alone — he is the only six-drop in the deck, he is not a source by himself, and after stack 001 he is a combo piece for two specific partners rather than a general-purpose infinite enabler. Ship one-landers even with a mox; a mox that finds no second land loses the commander. And treat hands whose only route is Scurry Oak, Ivy Lane Denizen or Host of the Hereafter as hands with *no* route, because those lines are unresolved and you should not mulligan-plan around a combo the pilot's manual will not assert.

On a mulligan to six, the priorities compress to exactly two things: lands that produce black on turn 2, and one card that either places counters repeatedly or finds one that does.
threat_assessment:
Start from the correction that reorganises everything else: Hapatra is not an engine, she is a mint. Her first ability is a combat-damage trigger on an unevasive 2/2 — verified stack 001 step 11 classifies it as "not an at-will repeatable placement" worth at most one extra iteration per combat — so she does not make -1/-1 counters, she monetises counters other cards place, one deathtouch Snake each. The scarce resource in this deck is therefore the counter SOURCE, not the outlet and not the payoff, and stack 001's census of every mana-free sacrifice outlet found eight of them (Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni, Yawgmoth, Blasting Station, Lazotep Quarry) with exactly one — Yawgmoth — that also places a counter. Everything downstream is abundant; the enabler class is two deep. Read your own hands and your tutors through that lens (strategy:mulligans.engine-hands: payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists), and read the table through it too.

Now the hardest thing to know about this deck, and the thing that should drive your threat ranking from the pre-game onward: your interaction covers exactly one of the five permanent classes. Eight removal slots, two sweepers and four protection slots all answer creatures. There is no artifact removal, no enchantment removal, no counterspell and no land answer, and the only graveyard-touching effect in the list is Abstergo Entertainment's {3}, {T}, exile-itself ability — which returns a historic card and exiles graveyards, and destroys nothing. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite is blunt about the cost: breadth before depth, because "three opponents mean every permanent type appears." So invert the usual habit. A creature is never the threat you should be most afraid of — you have eight answers and two sweepers for creatures, plus a board of deathtouch blockers. The threats that actually beat you are the ones you will never remove: a Sphere effect, Winter Orb, Blood Moon, a Rest-in-Peace-class hoser, a Rule-of-Law effect, an artifact or enchantment combo assembling in front of you. strategy:threat-assessment: "an answer only counts when it matches a threat that actually beats you." Rank by permanent class before you rank by size. If two seats can present prison permanents, your role is decided for you before the first land drop — you do not own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown racing the lock's completion (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial), and your outs are speed, politics and someone else's removal. Name them out loud on turn one and sequence to protect them (strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs).

What the table sees early is cheap and defensive, and that is a real asset. Hapatra costs two and lands on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 goldfish runs (mean cast turn 2.007, median 2, 99.9% by turn 6), and 'commander plus any -1/-1 payoff' assembles 67.2% of the time at a mean turn of 3.623, 55.7% by turn 6. A 2/2 Cleric and a couple of 1/1 Snakes read as a defensive board — exactly the posture strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection tells you to buy, engines that read as defensive while the spotlight sits on a scarier board. But this list spends that budget faster than most, and you need to know the exact moment it goes: the 11 Game Changers are the tell. Chrome Mox, Mox Diamond, Mana Vault, Grim Monolith, Demonic Tutor, Vampiric Tutor, Imperial Seal, Worldly Tutor, Survival of the Fittest, Orcish Bowmasters, The One Ring. The turn a Mox hits the battlefield or a Demonic Tutor resolves, the Snakes stop reading as chump blockers and start reading as a combo deck's early board, and the deflection budget is spent — strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection notes the table discounts your "I haven't done anything" precisely because it tracks mana and draw engines. Practical sequencing: lead with the token half and the cheap counter sources, deploy fast mana on the turn it actually buys you a threat rather than on turn one for its own sake, and fire tutors on a turn when someone else has just done something louder. The One Ring is the loudest card in the deck — it is a "does this win if it resolves" object in the table's eyes and it costs you escalating life every upkeep; cast it when you want the cards, not when you want the protection turn to look clever.

The flip from ignored to archenemy has three concrete triggers, and all three are the second permanent, never Hapatra herself. First: Yawgmoth plus a second body with Hapatra out. Stack 001 step 12 verifies the shape — pay 1 life, sacrifice another creature, put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw; targets are locked before costs are paid, but a target that has left the zone is illegal on resolution and the ability has a single instance of "target," so an illegal target means it does not resolve at all and you do not even draw. Hence the mandatory second body, and hence Hapatra's Snakes filling that slot. The A/B loop repeats for real but is library-bounded by its own mandatory draw — a strong engine, not a true infinite. Any competent opponent kills Yawgmoth on sight, so do not present him into open mana unless the turn converts. Second: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed alongside Devoted Druid — the deck's one verified true two-card infinite (stack 001 steps 13-14), of deaths, -1/-1 placements, Snakes and drain, explicitly NOT of mana: three green on the first pass and zero on every pass after, because the returned Druid is a new object and 302.6 blocks its tap ability. Steady state is four counter placements and one death per cycle at zero mana; with Blood Artist already on board it converts directly at one life per cycle from a player of your choice (step 16). Third: Mikaeus plus Walking Ballista plus any free outlet — genuinely unbounded, converts to damage with no drain payoff at all, and is a three-card assembly, because Mikaeus's +1/+1 is a layer-7c modification that makes a counterless Ballista a 1/1 and switches off the classic self-kill (step 15). Mikaeus costs six and goldfish mean available mana is 6.150 on turn 6; 'Mikaeus + a free sacrifice outlet' is drawn 9.5% of the time overall, 5.8% by turn 6, mean turn 5.092 — and that target now overstates its own value, because stack 001 refuted six of the eight Mikaeus entries it was built to track.

Which brings the last piece of threat management, the one aimed at your own self-image. The bracket-4 classification is safe — 11 Game Changers carry the floor by themselves — but the '19 two-card infinites' figure in the bracket report is inflated, and you should not repeat it in a Rule 0 conversation or believe it at the table. Two lines are verified (Mikaeus + Devoted Druid; Mikaeus + Walking Ballista, as a three-card assembly). Six are refuted outright by stack 001, checker verdict pass over four iterations: Mikaeus with Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni or Blasting Station each yield exactly one extra undying return, and Snake tokens yield zero, because a token in a zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist before its undying trigger is even placed on the stack. Eleven remain unresolved — the three Blowfly Infestation entries, Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen, the six outlet-paired Ivy Lane entries, and Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter. None of the eleven may be spoken of as fact or tapped out for. The Blowfly line in particular is the one goldfish tracks (16.3% assembled, 12.5% by turn 6, mean turn 4.102) and it is exactly the one with no stack scenario behind it, so treat it as a strong board rather than a kill until it is verified. Separate ceiling from median and pace for the median (strategy:critical-mass, strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density): the median is genuinely strong, and when you do choose to be the archenemy, take one counted pivot window rather than the first loop that looks like it works — strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window says assume every held answer appears the moment you present lethal, so count the table's open mana first and prefer the attempt that leaves Bitterblossom, Snakes and a drain converter behind if it fails.
upgrades:
Two honest notes before the list. First, the obsolescence index in this repository is a strict machine test — same supertype, tag superset, equal-or-lower mana value, equal-or-tighter color, equal-or-better stats, newer printing, at least one concrete advantage — and it is *silent* on almost every card in this deck. Several of the list's key pieces (Hapatra herself, Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, Walking Ballista, Blood Artist, Skullclamp) return no entry at all, which is the index saying no strictly-better card exists, not that they are unimprovable. Second, this deck has already been built to bracket 4 by the deterministic builder, so the ordinary 'run better tutors' advice is spent — all eight are in.

The upgrade that actually matters is not a card swap, it is a re-targeting. Stack 001's verified census changes what you fetch. Before it, the natural read of this list was 'find Mikaeus and any free sacrifice outlet' — a target the goldfish still tracks at 9.5%. After it, six of those eight pairings are refuted, and the correct default target is **a free repeatable -1/-1 source**: Yawgmoth first, Devoted Druid second and only alongside Mikaeus. Then a table-wide converter — Obelisk Spider, Zulaport Cutthroat or Bastion of Remembrance — and only then protection. If you change one thing about how you play this deck, change that ordering.

The genuine deckbuilding upgrade is breadth, and the strategic frame names it plainly: all fourteen interactive slots point at creatures. A scan of every card in the list confirms there is no artifact removal, no enchantment removal, no counterspell and no land answer, and the only graveyard interaction is Abstergo Entertainment's exile-itself ability. Against permanent-based prison or an artifact combo deck you have no line at all. The cheapest fix, in a deck whose worst cards are its narrowest counter sources, is to convert one or two of Contagion Clasp, Crumbling Ashes and Serrated Arrows into BG answers that hit noncreature permanents. That is a real trade — those three are counter sources, the scarce class — so it should be made with eyes open, and it is a Rule 0 conversation about your pod rather than a strict improvement.

The class-level upgrade inside the deck is converter quality. Blood Artist drains one *target player* per death; Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance and Obelisk Spider drain *each opponent*. In a four-player game that is a threefold difference on every trigger, and Obelisk Spider additionally fires on counter placement rather than on death, which is the faster clock on any counter loop. If you are adding converters rather than swapping them, add in that order.

Finally, an upgrade that is really a subtraction: stop counting nineteen infinites. Two are verified, six are refuted, and eleven are unresolved. Queue stack scenarios for the Blowfly family, the Mikaeus-anthem question (does his +1/+1 switch your own token loops off?), Scurry Oak + Ivy Lane Denizen and the six outlet-paired Ivy Lane entries, Hapatra + Host of the Hereafter, the Yawgmoth + Hapatra kill without Mikaeus, and Necroskitter + Black Sun's Zenith. Every one of those is a line this manual would happily print if a checker signed off on it, and until one does, the accurate self-description of this deck is a strong engine with a narrow verified ceiling — which is a better deck to pilot than a fictional one with nineteen kills.
